newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Russia, Ukraine resolve row over Black Sea fleet.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Ukraine resolve row over Black Sea fleet.

text.p: Russia and Ukraine have settled a longrunning dispute over a shareout of the former Soviet Black Sea fleet and the terms for its base at Sevastopol, Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Wednesday.

The accord beamed a green light for a bilateral summit between presidents Boris Yeltsin of Russia and Leonid Kuchma of Ukraine in Kiev on Friday. The summit had been repeatedly delayed by a welter of policy differences since the 1991 breakup of the Soviet Union.
Kuchma and Chernomyrdin said after a preparatory meeting that they had solved the most painful issues facing the two post-Soviet states.

"I have some good news for you," Kuchma, looking cheerful and relaxed, told senior Russian and Ukrainian officials after three hours of face-to-face talks with Chernomyrdin. "We have just solved all the problems," he said as reporters looked on.
Chernomyrdin made clear that the fleet dispute, the one which did most to sour relations between the two Slav states, had been overcome.

"We will sign documents today and I think all problems concerning the Black Sea Fleet will be solved," he told reporters as he visited a monument to Prince Yaroslav the Wise, the 12th century ruler of Kiev Rus which was the ancestor state of both Russia and Ukraine.
Interfax-Ukraine news agency quoted Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko as saying he and Chernomyrdin were planning to sign three deals on the fleet. Lazarenko did not elaborate.

Urkainian officials have said one of the three deals would set terms for basing Russian ships in Ukraine, a second would settle the division of the fleet and the third would spell out what Moscow would pay Kiev in rent for hosting its share.

Russia had insisted that Ukraine base its share of the ships 140 km (90 miles) north of Sevastopol. But sources close to the talks in Sevastopol said this week that the two sides had agreed to moor their vessels at different bays of the Ukrainian port.
Kuchma and Chernomyrdin met two days before Yeltsin was due to start a two-day visit to Kiev and sign a milestone friendship treaty.
"I think they (Kuchma and Yeltsin) will sign the document of the century," an upbeat Chernomyrdin told reporters.

Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze said on Wednesday the ex-Soviet republic also had a claim to some of the ships of the Black Sea Fleet which were based in the Georgian port of Poti before 1992, Itar-Tass news agency reported.
"Those ships of the former Soviet Black Sea Fleet were taken from Poti without consent and consultations with Georgian authorities," he told a news conference in Tbilisi, according to Itar-Tass.
Shevardnadze said he had sent two written messages to Yeltsin recently, calling his attention to Georgia's desire for part of the Black Sea Fleet, but had not received any written reply.
He said Georgia had helped create and maintain the fleet and had the right, as a Black Sea country, to some of its warships.
In Kiev, Kuchma's spokesman Dmytro Markov told reporters the Ukrainian leader and the Russian premier had managed to solve another tricky issue -- bilateral trade.
"The sides have voiced concern over a dramatic decline in trade turnover and decided to lift all barriers which stand in the way of bilateral trade," Markov said.
He gave no details, but Kiev has complained about what it saw as discriminatory Russian policies while Moscow accused Ukraine of dumping cheap and poor quality goods on its market.
Yeltsin had cancelled six visits to sign the friendship treaty but with Moscow busy shaping new relations with the West, settling old grievances with Ukraine is in the Kremlin's interest.

Yeltsin and leaders of NATO countries signed a historic pact on Tuesday under which Moscow acquired some say in the Western defence alliance in exchange for acceptance of its plans to admit several eastern European countries.

The Kremlin, which had hailed the deal with NATO as an end to confrontation in Europe, is nevertheless worried by prospects of any further advance eastwards by NATO to countries which once were part of the Soviet Union.

Russian officials have said Moscow wanted to encourage Ukraine to stick to plans to sign a special deal with NATO rather then seek membership in the alliance like the three Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia.
